reasoning.snell: For the ordinary transparent isotropic media of this lesson, n1 sin(alpha)=n2 sin(beta). Away from zero this gives unchanged 6.8/6.10; n=n2/n1 is unchanged 6.9. At alpha=beta=0 use the undivided law or unchanged 6.11, never 0/0.
reasoning.angleInequality: n2>n1 and positive incidence yield sin(beta)<sin(alpha); both angles are acute, so beta<alpha. At normal incidence both zero. Author explicitly scopes this to oblique air-to-glass/water.
reasoning.dispersion: Normal dispersion means n decreases as wavelength increases in the stated transparent visible range. Red has longer wavelength than green and green than violet, so the retained order follows. No universal order across arbitrary absorbing/anomalous ranges is claimed.
reasoning.air: Retained source standard-state yellow-light approximation 1.000292 is close to, not exactly, 1. Consequently n2/n1 approximately n2; no new numeric measurement or universal exact index introduced.
reasoning.reflectionIndependentDerivation: For an ordinary lossless nonmagnetic air-to-water/glass interface, write Rs=[(n1 cos(alpha)-n2 cos(beta))/(n1 cos(alpha)+n2 cos(beta))]^2 and Rp=[(n2 cos(alpha)-n1 cos(beta))/(n2 cos(alpha)+n1 cos(beta))]^2, with Snell's transmitted beta. Unpolarized reflectance is (Rs+Rp)/2. Rp can vanish at Brewster incidence, so a polarized beam need not strengthen monotonically. The ordinary unpolarized air-to-water/glass beam has the stated overall strengthening trend. As alpha tends to 90 degrees, cos(alpha) tends to zero while cos(beta) stays positive (n2>n1), so both Rs and Rp tend to 1. This is a grazing limit, not TIR: n1 sin(alpha)<n2 and a real transmitted angle exists below grazing. These formulas are reviewer reasoning, not additions to candidate text and not a script/native test.
reasoning.stateAndTerminology: Optical density comparison is refractive-index comparison, not mass density. Physical-state dependence, including elastic stress, remains. Omitted table conditions are neglected only in the stated approximation.

Brewster's relation uses n2/n1. It also discusses stress- and wavelength-dependent optical behavior.
